title: Who Owns Your AI Workflows?
summary: OpenAI acknowledged it cannot rule out that a mathematician's private research notes used in Codex may have helped improve their models, and that single statement captures the ownership problem most enterprises have not fully confronted. The question is not whether your AI provider will misuse your data but whether you can answer basic questions about where it goes, who sees it, and whether it stays yours.
body_markdown:
Artificial intelligence is moving quickly, and the pace of progress is exciting. OpenAI recently demonstrated this by solving the Navier Stokes problem in just 88 hours, a remarkable achievement that shows what advanced AI systems can accomplish.


But the story also raises a more difficult question: what happens to the information people use while working with these systems?


Tristan Buckmaster, the NYU mathematician working on the same problem, had been keeping his notes in Codex. OpenAI later stated: “While unlikely, we cannot rule out that de-identified data derived from their usage of our products helped improve our models.”


That statement is important because it highlights a concern many organizations are beginning to confront. The question is not only whether an AI model can solve a complex problem. It is also whether the prompts, notes, workflows, and internal information used to reach that result remain under the organization’s control.


## The hidden cost of convenience


Proprietary AI tools are convenient. Employees can open a familiar interface, submit a prompt, upload information, and receive a useful result in seconds. This ease of use is one of the reasons AI adoption is spreading so quickly across organizations.


However, convenience can make it easy to overlook what happens to the information submitted along the way.


Employees may use internal documents, customer information, research notes, operational procedures, or proprietary workflows to get better results from an AI system. Even when the intention is harmless, organizations may not always have complete visibility into how that data is handled, retained, or used under changing terms and conditions.


This creates an uncomfortable gap between how employees experience AI and how organizations manage risk. To an employee, a prompt may feel like a temporary request. To the organization, that same prompt may contain valuable intellectual property, sensitive context, or a repeatable process that took years to develop.


## The problem with uncertainty


The challenge is not necessarily that every proprietary AI provider will misuse customer data. The challenge is uncertainty.


Terms and conditions can change. Product policies can evolve. Different AI tools can apply different rules to prompts, uploaded files, and model improvement. Organizations may also adopt multiple internal AI solutions, each with its own configuration and governance model.


As the number of tools increases, so does the difficulty of answering basic ownership questions:


- Where does our data go?
- Who can access it?
- How long is it retained?
- Can information derived from our usage contribute to future model improvements?
- Do our employees know which tools are approved for internal work?
- Can we audit the prompts and workflows being used across the organization?


When these questions do not have clear answers, organizations are left with lingering doubt. They may benefit from AI’s capabilities while remaining unsure whether their most valuable knowledge is staying within their boundaries.


## Private AI changes the ownership model


Privately hosted, fully owned AI offers a different approach.


Instead of sending sensitive prompts and workflows into an external service, organizations can operate AI in an environment they control. This can make it easier to define access rules, manage data handling, protect internal processes, and establish clear ownership over the systems being used.


Private AI does not remove the need for responsible governance. Organizations still need policies, security controls, monitoring, and clear guidance for employees. What it can do is reduce the uncertainty surrounding where data goes and how it may be used.


That distinction becomes increasingly important as AI moves from experimentation into everyday business operations. The more deeply AI is integrated into an organization’s workflows, the more important it becomes to know who controls the underlying models, prompts, and information.


## AI progress and AI ownership


The progress of AI is worth celebrating. Solving a complex mathematical problem in a matter of hours demonstrates the extraordinary potential of these systems.


At the same time, progress should not require organizations to give up ownership of the information that makes their AI workflows valuable.


The next stage of enterprise AI will not be defined only by which model produces the most impressive answer. It will also be defined by whether organizations can use AI while maintaining control over their data, their processes, and the knowledge embedded in their prompts.


Privately hosted, fully owned AI provides one path toward that goal. It offers organizations a way to benefit from advanced AI capabilities while reducing the uncertainty around data ownership and model usage.


**The question is no longer simply what AI can do. It is also who owns the work that makes those results possible.**
